title: Time & Home Management
subtitle: Plan your week, run your home with simple systems, and protect your rest, even with a family and a business to manage.

Sort tasks with the Eisenhower matrix and plan each week around your most important tasks
Set up morning and evening routines, a weekly cleaning schedule and a family chore chart

Separate business and household time and money, and set clear boundaries with family and customers
Keep your systems working with weekly, monthly and quarterly reviews

modules.title: Understanding Your Time
modules.overview: Before you can plan well, you need an honest picture of where your hours go. In this module you count the hours in your week, run a seven-day time audit, find the habits and situations that drain your time and energy, and build the first small habits of taking charge.

lessons.title: Your 168-Hour Week: Fixed Time, Flexible Time and Energy
objectives: Calculate how many hours in your week are already committed
Separate fixed time from flexible time in your own week
Explain why energy matters as much as hours
Describe the difference between a reactive day and a planned day

blocks.text: Every week has exactly **168 hours** (7 days x 24 hours). Nobody gets more. What differs from one woman to another is how much of that time is already spoken for, and how much is left for the things she chooses. This lesson helps you see your week as a set of numbers you can work with, instead of a blur of tiredness.

blocks.name: time-management
blocks.alt: A woman standing beside a large clock and a calendar
blocks.caption: Seeing your week as 168 hours turns a vague feeling of having no time into numbers you can plan with.

blocks.text: Fixed time and flexible time

**Fixed time** is time you cannot easily move: sleep, your job or shop hours, the school run, travel in traffic, cooking the main meal, worship services you attend every week. **Flexible time** is everything else: scrolling, visiting, extra chores, rest, learning, side projects. Most women discover that their flexible time is smaller than they hoped, but also larger than it feels, because much of it leaks away in small pieces of 10 and 20 minutes.

items: **Sleep:** most adults need 7 or more hours a night, so plan about 49 to 56 hours a week.
**Work or business:** shop hours, office hours, or the time you spend producing and delivering goods.
**Travel:** school runs, going to market, commuting. In big cities like Lagos or Abuja this can be 10 or more hours a week.
**Home basics:** cooking, washing up, laundry, fetching or storing water, cleaning.
**Care:** bathing small children, homework help, caring for an elderly parent.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting a real week
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small provisions shop in Enugu and has two children in primary school. She writes down her fixed hours with a pencil.
steps: Sleep: 7 hours x 7 nights = 49 hours.
Shop: 9 hours x 6 days = 54 hours.
School run and market trips: about 1.5 hours x 6 days = 9 hours.
Cooking, washing up and laundry: about 2.5 hours x 7 days = 17.5 hours.
Church on Sunday and midweek service: about 5 hours.
Total fixed time: 49 + 54 + 9 + 17.5 + 5 = 134.5 hours. Flexible time: 168 minus 134.5 = 33.5 hours.
blocks.result: Ngozi has about 33 flexible hours a week, roughly 4 to 5 hours a day. She had believed she had none. Now she can decide what those hours are for.

blocks.text: Hours are not all equal: energy

An hour at 6 am after good sleep is not the same as an hour at 10 pm after a long day in the shop. Your **energy** rises and falls during the day. Many people think most clearly in the morning, but some are sharper later. Notice when you feel alert and when you feel drained. Use your best-energy hours for work that needs thinking (accounts, planning, learning, important conversations) and your low-energy hours for simple tasks (folding clothes, sorting beans, replying to easy messages).

blocks.title: Find your best hours
blocks.text: For three days, write a number from 1 (exhausted) to 5 (fresh and focused) next to each two-hour block of your day. Look for the pattern. Protect your 4s and 5s for your most important tasks.
Reactive days and planned days

A **reactive** day is run by whatever shouts loudest: a phone call, a neighbour at the gate, a customer on WhatsApp, a child who suddenly needs something for school tomorrow. A **planned** day still has surprises, but you have already decided your top tasks and left some space for interruptions. You do not need to plan every minute. Even deciding three things the night before changes how the day feels.

blocks.title: Reactive day vs planned day
items: Reactive day
Planned day
right: Ends tired, but key work done
blocks.caption: Both days are busy; the planned day simply decides in advance what matters most.

blocks.text: Common mindsets that shrink your time

items: **'I have no time.'** Said often, it stops you looking for the hours you do have. Replace it with 'This is not a priority this week', which is usually more honest.
**Busyness as proof of worth.** Being seen to rush about can feel like being a good wife, mother or worker. But busy and effective are different things.
**Perfectionism.** Spending an hour making something perfect when ten minutes would make it good enough. Ask: what level of quality does this task really need?
**Saying yes to everyone.** Every yes to someone else uses hours from your 168. You will learn kind ways to say no in Module 2.

blocks.text: None of these mindsets make you a bad person; they are common habits of thinking. Simply noticing which one you fall into most is the first step to changing it.

In the rest of this course you will build the tools for planned days: an audit of where your time goes, a way to choose priorities, a weekly plan, home routines, shared chores, meal and money planning, and boundaries that protect your rest.

takeaways: Every week has 168 hours; count your fixed hours to find your flexible ones.
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep, so plan for it rather than squeezing it.
Match tasks to energy: thinking work in your best hours, simple work in low hours.
A planned day still has surprises, but it starts with your top three tasks.

activity.title: Count your week
steps: On a sheet of paper, write the seven categories: sleep, work or business, travel, home basics, care, worship or community, other fixed time.
Estimate the hours per day for each and multiply to get weekly totals.
Add up your fixed time and subtract it from 168.
Write your flexible hours in a circle at the top of the page.
Rate your energy 1 to 5 for each two-hour block of tomorrow.
activity.evidence: A photo of your 168-hour sheet showing fixed hours, flexible hours and your energy ratings.

lessons.title: The Seven-Day Time Audit: Where Your Hours Really Go
objectives: Record your activities in 30-minute blocks for seven days
Group your activities into clear categories and total them
Spot the gap between where you think time goes and where it goes
Choose one change based on your audit results

blocks.text: In the last lesson you estimated your week. Estimates are useful, but memory is not reliable: we forget the 20 minutes spent searching for keys or the hour that disappeared on WhatsApp statuses. A **time audit** means writing down what you actually did, as you go, for one full week. It is the single most useful thing you can do before making any plan.

blocks.name: stopwatch
blocks.caption: A time audit measures your real week, in small blocks, instead of relying on memory.

blocks.text: How to run the audit

items: Choose a normal week, not a festive season or a week when you are travelling.
Prepare a log: a notebook page per day with times down the side from waking to sleeping, in 30-minute rows. A phone notes app works too.
Every two or three hours, stop and fill in what you did in each 30-minute block. Do not wait until night.
Be honest. Write 'phone, TikTok' or 'chatting with neighbour' if that is what happened. Nobody else needs to see it.
At the end of each day, mark each block with a category letter.

blocks.text: Categories that work well

head: Letter
Category
Examples
rows: Shop, office, making products, deliveries, customer messages
Cooking, cleaning, laundry, market, water, repairs
Children, homework, elderly parent, sick family member
Traffic, bus queues, waiting at the bank or hospital
Social media, videos, browsing, long chats
Sleep, naps, exercise, prayer, reading, hobbies
Visits, events, meetings, church or mosque groups

blocks.title: Use your phone's own records
blocks.text: For the phone category, check your real screen time. On most Android phones open Settings, then Digital Wellbeing and parental controls. On an iPhone open Settings, then Screen Time. Both show hours per day and which apps used them.
Analysing your results

After seven days, count the blocks for each letter and divide by two to get hours. Then compare with what you guessed in Lesson 1.1. Look for three things: the biggest category you did not expect, the times of day when your time leaks the most, and any tasks that keep being repeated because they were not finished properly the first time.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading an audit
blocks.context: For example, Halima is a teacher in Kaduna who also bakes cakes to order. She guessed she spent about 1 hour a day on her phone outside work.
steps: Her log shows 46 blocks of P (phone) across the week: 46 / 2 = 23 hours, about 3.3 hours a day.
T (travel and waiting) totals 18 blocks = 9 hours, mostly waiting at the bank and in traffic on Fridays.
H (home) shows the same task, 'looking for ingredients I thought I had', appearing four times.
She compares: guessed 7 hours of phone a week, actual 23. The gap is 16 hours.
She decides on one change: no social media before her baking orders are done, using an app timer.
blocks.result: By acting on one clear finding, Halima wins back several hours a week for her cake orders without giving up her phone completely.

blocks.title: Time audit in five steps
items: Log in 30-minute blocks
Label each block
Total hours by category
Compare with your guess
Pick one change
blocks.caption: The audit only helps if it ends with one specific change you start this week.

blocks.text: Common surprises

items: Phone time is usually two to three times higher than people guess.
Waiting (queues, power cuts, late visitors) adds up to more than expected. Waiting time can be used for small tasks like planning or reading.
Small unplanned market trips (for one missing item) cost a lot of travel time. A weekly list fixes much of this.
Rest is often almost missing. That is a warning sign, not a badge of honour.

blocks.title: Be kind to yourself
blocks.text: The audit is information, not a judgement. Its purpose is to show you where change is possible. Many women find that just keeping the log makes them use time more carefully during that week.

Also look at the **shape** of your days, not only the totals. Are mornings calm and evenings chaotic, or the other way round? Is Saturday overloaded with all the cleaning, laundry and visits? Which day of the week is lightest? These patterns tell you where to place important tasks when you plan your week in Module 2.
If a full week feels too much

If seven days of logging feels impossible, log three days: two weekdays and one weekend day. The picture will be less complete but still useful. Another option is to set a phone alarm every two hours labelled 'log', so you remember. If you cannot read or write easily, you can record a short voice note on WhatsApp to yourself each time, then count the categories with a family member at the end of the day.

takeaways: Memory underestimates small time leaks; a written log shows the truth.
Log in 30-minute blocks, labelled with simple category letters.
Check real screen time in Digital Wellbeing (Android) or Screen Time (iPhone).
Finish the audit by choosing one specific change.

activity.title: Run your audit
steps: Set up a seven-day log with 30-minute rows from waking to sleeping.
Fill it in every two or three hours for seven days.
Label each block with W, H, C, T, P, R or S.
Total the hours per category and compare with your Lesson 1.1 estimate.
Write down the biggest surprise and one change you will make.
activity.evidence: Your completed seven-day log (photos of the pages) and a one-page summary of totals, surprise and chosen change.

lessons.title: Time Wasters and Energy Drains, and How to Reduce Them
objectives: Name the most common time wasters in a busy household and business
Use phone settings to limit distracting apps
Reduce interruptions and repeated trips with simple systems
Identify energy drains such as poor sleep, skipped meals and clutter

blocks.text: Your audit has probably shown some leaks. This lesson names the usual culprits and gives a fix for each. You will not remove every waster, and you do not need to. Cutting two or three of the biggest ones can free several hours a week.

blocks.name: mobile-phone
blocks.caption: The phone is both a work tool and the biggest time leak for many women; settings can help you control it.

blocks.text: The phone

Your phone is where customers find you, where your children's school sends messages and where family news arrives. It is also designed to keep you scrolling. The goal is not to throw it away but to decide when you use it for what.

items: **App timers:** Android's Digital Wellbeing lets you set a daily limit per app. iPhone's Screen Time has App Limits. When the limit is reached, the app pauses.
**Bedtime or Downtime modes:** schedule your phone to go quiet and grey at night so you sleep instead of scrolling.
**Turn off non-essential notifications:** keep calls, family and customer chats; switch off group chat and social media alerts.
**Mute busy WhatsApp groups:** open the group, tap its name, choose Mute notifications. Read them once a day at a set time.
**Batch replies:** answer non-urgent messages at two or three fixed times a day instead of every few minutes.

blocks.text: Interruptions and unclear tasks

Each interruption costs more than its own length, because it takes time to get back into what you were doing. Common ones are visitors without notice, children calling 'Mummy!' for things they can do themselves, and calls that could have been a message. Unclear tasks also waste time: 'sort out the house' is hard to start, while 'clear and wipe the kitchen table' is easy.

head: Time waster
Simple fix
rows: One fixed place for each: a hook for keys, a folder for documents
Several market trips for forgotten items
A running shopping list on the fridge or in your phone
Agree visiting times with close friends and family
Re-doing tasks done badly in a hurry
Finish one task properly before starting another
Waiting in queues or during power cuts
Keep a small 'waiting list' of tasks: plan the week, read, review accounts
Long phone calls about small things
Say kindly: 'I am in the middle of work, can we talk at 7?'

blocks.title: Worked example: cutting three wasters
blocks.context: For example, Funke sells fabrics from home in Ibadan. Her audit showed 2.5 hours a day on the phone outside sales, about 1 hour a day looking for things, and three market trips a week for forgotten items.
steps: She sets a 45-minute daily limit on Facebook and TikTok in Digital Wellbeing.
She buys two hooks and a box file: keys on the hooks, receipts and school papers in the file.
She sticks a list on the fridge and only goes to market once a week with it.
After two weeks she re-checks: phone outside sales down to about 1 hour a day, searching down to about 15 minutes, market trips down to one.
blocks.result: Funke wins back roughly 2 hours a day plus two market trips a week, which she uses for sales follow-up and an earlier bedtime.

blocks.text: Energy drains

Sometimes the problem is not time but energy. You have the hour but feel too tired to use it. Common energy drains are short sleep, skipping breakfast and then eating heavy food late, not drinking enough water in the heat, a cluttered room that makes every task slower, and unresolved worries that keep the mind busy. Writing worries down, even as a list, often reduces their hold.

blocks.title: Daily energy check
items: Slept 7 or more hours
Ate a proper breakfast
Drank water through the day
Workspace cleared
Worries written down
blocks.caption: Tick these each evening for a week; low-energy days usually miss two or more.

blocks.text: Clutter: the hidden time cost

Clutter slows every task: you move things before you can cook, you search before you can dress the children, you clean around piles instead of cleaning the surface. Start small. Clear one surface a day, such as the kitchen counter, the dining table or the top of the fridge. Ask of each item: do we use this? If not, give it away, sell it or throw it away. Keep a box by the door for items going out of the house.

blocks.title: When tiredness does not go away
blocks.text: If you feel exhausted most days even after rest, or feel low for weeks, see a doctor or health worker. Ongoing tiredness can have medical causes, such as anaemia, that need checking.

takeaways: Fix the two or three biggest leaks from your audit first.
Use app timers, bedtime modes and muted groups to control the phone.
Give every item a fixed home and keep a running shopping list.
Energy drains like short sleep and clutter waste time too.

activity.title: Fix three leaks
steps: From your audit, list your top three time wasters.
Write a specific fix next to each, using the table in this lesson.
Set at least one app limit or mute at least three busy WhatsApp groups.
Keep your daily energy check for seven evenings.
After one week, note how much time each fix saved.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your app limit or muted groups, and a note listing your three fixes and the time saved.

lessons.title: From Busy to In Charge: Habits of Time Ownership
objectives: Explain Parkinson's law and use deadlines to your advantage
Apply time blocking, batching and the two-minute rule
Build a new habit by attaching it to an existing one
Run a simple weekly review of what worked

blocks.text: Taking charge of time is less about willpower and more about a few habits that make good choices easy. This lesson gives you five practical habits used by busy people around the world, adapted for home and small business life.

blocks.name: focus
blocks.alt: A woman working with focus at a desk
blocks.caption: A protected block of focused time often achieves more than a whole day of scattered effort.

blocks.text: 1. Use Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time

In 1955 the British writer C. Northcote Parkinson observed that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion'. If you give yourself all morning to clean the house, it will take all morning. If you decide it will take 60 minutes and set a timer, it often does. Give tasks a time limit, especially chores and admin.
2. Time blocking

**Time blocking** means giving a task a specific slot on your calendar, like an appointment: 'Tuesday 6:00 to 7:00 am, do the shop accounts.' A task with a time is far more likely to happen than a task on a list. Start with one or two blocks a day, in your best-energy hours.
3. Batching

**Batching** means doing similar tasks together. Reply to all customer messages at 12 noon. Do all the ironing on one evening when there is power. Cook two stews at once and freeze one. Every switch between different tasks costs time, so grouping them saves it.
4. The two-minute rule
Batching also works for errands. Plan one route that covers the bank, the tailor and the pharmacy on the same afternoon, instead of three separate trips across town in traffic.

From David Allen's book *Getting Things Done*: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it now instead of writing it down. Hang the towel, reply 'Yes, I will be there', put the receipt in the file. Small tasks left undone pile up into a heavy load.
5. Habit stacking

New habits stick better when you attach them to something you already do every day. The formula is: **After I [current habit], I will [new habit].** For example: 'After I make my morning tea, I will look at my top three tasks.' 'After I lock the shop, I will write tomorrow's list.'

blocks.title: Worked example: one week of new habits
blocks.context: For example, Chioma is a hairdresser in Port Harcourt with a salon and three children. She chooses two habits for one week.
steps: Habit stack: after she puts the children to bed, she spends 10 minutes writing tomorrow's top three tasks.
Time block: Monday and Thursday, 7:00 to 8:00 am before opening, she orders stock and updates her records.
Batching: she replies to booking messages at 10 am, 2 pm and 6 pm instead of throughout the day.
Two-minute rule: she clears small salon tasks (wiping a chair, filing a receipt) immediately.
On Sunday evening she reviews: the evening list happened 6 nights out of 7; stock was ordered on time both days.
blocks.result: Chioma finishes stock orders on time for the first time in months and feels less scattered, using only about 2.5 hours of planned time a week.

blocks.title: The weekly ownership cycle
items: Plan the week
Block key tasks
Do and batch
Review on Sunday
Adjust and repeat
blocks.caption: Ownership grows from a small cycle repeated every week, not from one perfect plan.

blocks.text: The weekly review

Once a week, spend 15 minutes answering three questions in a notebook: What went well? What did not happen, and why? What will I change next week? This short review is what turns the habits into lasting change. You will build on it in Module 2.
Paper or phone?

Use whichever tool you will actually open every day. A cheap notebook and pen works well and needs no data or charge. If you prefer your phone, Google Calendar is free on Android and lets you set reminders for time blocks; Google Keep or your phone's notes app is enough for lists. Avoid using several tools at once, or tasks get lost between them. Whatever you choose, keep it in the same place every day so it becomes part of your routine.
If a habit fails for a few days, do not start again from zero in your mind. Simply do it today. Missing one day makes little difference; giving up after one miss is what breaks habits.

Measure progress honestly. A good sign is not that every day goes to plan, but that your most important tasks get done more often than before, and that you end the week with fewer surprises and less last-minute rushing.

blocks.title: Start with two habits, not five
blocks.text: Trying everything at once usually fails by Wednesday. Choose the two habits that would help you most, keep them for two weeks, then add another.

takeaways: Give tasks time limits: work expands to fill the time available.
A task with a time slot is more likely to happen than one on a list.
Batch similar tasks and do anything under two minutes straight away.
Attach new habits to old ones, and review weekly.

activity.title: Two habits for two weeks
steps: Choose two of the five habits from this lesson.
Write each as a specific sentence, for example 'After I lock the shop, I will write tomorrow's top three'.
Make a simple tracker with 14 boxes for each habit.
Tick each day you do it.
At the end of each week, answer the three review questions.
activity.evidence: A photo of your habit tracker and your two weekly review notes.

quiz.q: Amina sleeps 7 hours a night, works 50 hours a week, travels 8 hours a week and spends 20 hours a week on home tasks and care. About how many flexible hours does she have?
quiz.explain: Sleep is 49 hours. 49 + 50 + 8 + 20 = 127 fixed hours. 168 minus 127 = 41 flexible hours.

quiz.q: During her time audit, Grace guessed she used social media 1 hour a day. What is the best way to check the real figure?
options: Check Digital Wellbeing or Screen Time in her phone settings
Assume it is double her guess
quiz.explain: Android's Digital Wellbeing and iPhone's Screen Time record actual hours per app, which is far more reliable than memory.

quiz.q: Which task is best placed in your highest-energy hours?
options: Working out the shop's monthly accounts
quiz.explain: Thinking work such as accounts needs your sharpest attention; simple tasks can go in low-energy hours.

quiz.q: Bisi goes to market three times a week because she keeps forgetting items. Which fix from the course addresses this directly?
options: A running shopping list and one planned weekly trip
quiz.explain: Repeated trips for forgotten items are fixed by a running list and one planned market trip.

quiz.q: Ada writes: 'After I make my morning tea, I will review my top three tasks.' Which habit technique is this?
quiz.explain: Habit stacking attaches a new habit to an existing daily one using the 'After I..., I will...' formula.

quiz.q: Kemi gives herself the whole Saturday to clean, and it takes the whole Saturday. Which idea explains this?
quiz.explain: Parkinson's law says work expands to fill the time available; setting a time limit usually shortens the task.

modules.title: Planning and Prioritising
modules.overview: This module turns awareness into a plan. You will sort tasks with the urgent-important (Eisenhower) matrix, run a weekly planning session and a short daily plan, set realistic goals with timelines, and learn respectful ways to say no so your plan survives contact with real life.

lessons.title: The Eisenhower Matrix: Sorting Urgent from Important
objectives: Explain the difference between urgent and important tasks
Sort a real task list into the four quadrants of the Eisenhower matrix
Decide what to do now, schedule, delegate or drop
Protect time for important but not urgent tasks

blocks.text: When everything feels like it must be done today, you need a quick way to decide what comes first. The **Eisenhower matrix**, also called the urgent-important matrix, is one of the simplest and best-known tools for this. It is named after Dwight D. Eisenhower, the American general and president, and was made popular by Stephen Covey's book *The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People*.

blocks.name: prioritise
blocks.alt: A person arranging tasks in order of priority
blocks.caption: Sorting tasks by urgency and importance tells you which to do now and which to schedule, delegate or drop.

blocks.text: Two questions for every task

items: **Is it urgent?** Does it need attention now or very soon, with a real consequence if it waits? A customer order due at 4 pm today, a child with a high fever, a bill that will cause a disconnection tomorrow.
**Is it important?** Does it move you towards your goals, protect your family's health, income or wellbeing? Saving for school fees, learning a new skill, checking your business records, rest.

blocks.text: Urgent things shout; important things often whisper. Many urgent things are not important (a ringing phone, a forwarded message asking you to share it now), and many important things are never urgent until it is too late (a health check, a savings plan, servicing the generator).

blocks.title: The Eisenhower matrix
items: Do now: urgent, important
Schedule: important, not urgent
Delegate: urgent, not important
Drop: neither
blocks.caption: Top row is important, left column is urgent; aim to spend more time in the 'Schedule' box so fewer things become emergencies.

blocks.text: What to do in each quadrant

head: Quadrant
Action
Home and business examples
rows: Child sick, order due today, rent deadline tomorrow, leaking pipe
Weekly planning, savings, learning, exercise, health check, stock records, family time
Most calls and messages, some errands, buying bread, some requests from others
Endless scrolling, forwarding chain messages, long gossip, watching another episode

blocks.text: The key insight is quadrant 2. When you schedule important tasks before they become urgent, quadrant 1 shrinks. For example, servicing the generator on a planned Saturday (quadrant 2) prevents a breakdown on the night before an exam (quadrant 1). Buying school uniforms in the holidays prevents the rush on resumption day.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting a Monday list
blocks.context: For example, Joy runs a small catering business in Abuja and has ten things on her list on Monday morning.
steps: Q1 Do now: deliver the small chops order due at 1 pm; pay the electricity token before tonight; collect her son's medicine.
Q2 Schedule: update her price list (Wednesday 7 am); plan next week's menu (Saturday 6 pm); open a savings account for equipment (Thursday lunchtime).
Q3 Delegate: buying soft drinks for the order (her assistant); replying to price enquiries (copy-paste her saved quick reply once at noon).
Q4 Drop: watching a long video someone sent; joining a new WhatsApp group about a party she will not attend.
She does the three Q1 tasks by 1:30 pm, then puts the Q2 tasks into her calendar with times.
blocks.result: Joy finishes the urgent work early and, for the first time in weeks, has the important but easy-to-postpone tasks booked into her week.

blocks.title: Delegating is not dumping
blocks.text: When you delegate, give clear instructions: what, by when, and what 'done' looks like. For example: 'Please buy 2 crates of Coke and 1 pack of water from the shop before 11 am, and keep the receipt.' Check once, kindly, then trust the person.
Common mistakes

items: Putting everything in quadrant 1. Ask honestly: what happens if this waits until tomorrow?
Never giving anything to quadrant 3 because 'nobody does it like me'. Accept good enough from others for low-importance tasks.
Treating other people's urgency as your own. A friend's last-minute request is urgent to her; it may not be important to you.
Leaving quadrant 2 empty. Book at least one quadrant 2 task every day, even 20 minutes.

blocks.text: Using the matrix every day

You do not need to draw the full matrix every morning. Once you are used to it, a quick mark next to each item on your list is enough: 1, 2, 3 or 4. Do the 1s first, give each 2 a time, hand over or batch the 3s, and cross out the 4s. Redo the full matrix at your weekly planning session, when you have more time to think.

Remember that importance depends on your goals. Joining a cooperative meeting may be quadrant 2 for a woman building a business and quadrant 4 for someone else. Decide based on what matters to you and your family this season, not on what others think should matter.

takeaways: Urgent means it needs attention soon; important means it serves your goals and wellbeing.
Do quadrant 1, schedule quadrant 2, delegate quadrant 3, drop quadrant 4.
Scheduling quadrant 2 tasks early shrinks future emergencies.
Delegate with clear instructions: what, by when, what done looks like.

activity.title: Sort your real list
steps: Write down every task on your mind right now, at least 12 items.
Draw the four-box matrix on a page.
Place each task in a box by asking the two questions.
Give each quadrant 2 task a day and time this week.
Choose one quadrant 3 task to delegate and one quadrant 4 task to drop.
activity.evidence: A photo of your completed matrix with times written next to each quadrant 2 task.

lessons.title: Weekly and Daily Planning That Survives Real Life
objectives: Run a 30-minute weekly planning session
Place your most important tasks first, then fit smaller tasks around them
Write a daily plan with a top three and buffer time
Adjust your plan when power cuts, visitors or emergencies happen

blocks.text: A plan does not need to be fancy. It needs to be made regularly, kept in one place and flexible enough to bend when life happens. This lesson gives you a simple weekly session and a five-minute daily plan that work together.

blocks.name: calendar
blocks.alt: A person marking dates on a large calendar
blocks.caption: A short weekly planning session places your important tasks on specific days before the week fills up.

blocks.text: The weekly planning session (30 minutes)

Choose a fixed time each week, for example Sunday evening after the children are in bed, or Saturday morning before the market. Sit with your notebook or calendar, last week's notes and your task list.

items: **Review last week (5 minutes):** what got done, what did not, and why.
**List fixed commitments (5 minutes):** work hours, school events, appointments, worship, deliveries, family events. Write them on the days.
**Choose your 'big rocks' (5 minutes):** the three to five most important tasks for the week, mostly quadrant 2 tasks from the Eisenhower matrix.
**Place big rocks first (5 minutes):** give each one a day and a time, in your best-energy hours if possible.
**Add home rhythm (5 minutes):** market day, laundry day, cooking and batch-cooking days, cleaning tasks.
**Leave buffer (5 minutes):** keep at least one free hour on most days for the unexpected.

blocks.text: The idea of 'big rocks' is often explained with a jar: if you pour in sand and pebbles first, the big rocks do not fit; if you put the big rocks in first, the pebbles and sand settle around them. Your important tasks are the rocks. Small tasks will always find space.

blocks.title: Weekly planning session
items: Review last week
Write fixed commitments
Choose 3 to 5 big rocks
Place big rocks first
Add home rhythm
Leave buffer time
blocks.caption: Thirty minutes once a week, in this order, gives your week a shape before others fill it.

blocks.text: The daily plan (5 minutes)

Each evening, or first thing in the morning, look at the weekly plan and write your **top three** for the day: the three tasks that would make the day a success if nothing else got done. Then list smaller tasks underneath. Do at least one of the top three before you open social media.

blocks.title: Worked example: a weekly plan
blocks.context: For example, Aisha works as a nurse on day shifts in Kano (Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday) and sells perfume oils on WhatsApp. On Sunday evening she plans her week.
steps: Fixed: shifts 7 am to 3 pm on four days; PTA meeting Wednesday 4 pm; family visit Saturday afternoon.
Big rocks: restock perfume oils; post a new product catalogue; take her daughter for an eye test; pay school fees instalment.
She places them: eye test Wednesday 10 am (day off); restock Wednesday 1 pm; catalogue post Thursday 7 pm; school fees by bank app Monday evening.
Home rhythm: market Saturday 8 am; laundry Wednesday morning when power is usually on; cook and freeze two stews Sunday.
Buffer: she leaves Friday evening free.
blocks.result: All four big rocks are done by Thursday night. When her shift runs late on Friday, nothing important is lost because Friday evening was buffer.

blocks.text: When the plan breaks

items: **Power cut:** swap tasks. Do tasks that need no power (planning, sorting, market) and move ironing or blending to when power returns.
**Unexpected visitors or a family emergency:** move today's top three to tomorrow's top three. Do not try to do everything late at night.
**Sick day:** cancel all but quadrant 1 tasks. Rest is the most important task when you are unwell.
**Task took longer than planned:** note it. Next time, plan more time for that kind of task.

blocks.title: Use reminders
blocks.text: In Google Calendar you can add a reminder to any event, such as 30 minutes before. For recurring tasks like 'pay rent' or 'buy gas', set them to repeat monthly so you never need to remember them yourself.
Keep your plan visible. A paper weekly plan on the fridge also helps your family see what is happening, which makes sharing tasks easier (Module 3).
Planning as a family

If you share a home, spend five minutes of your weekly session with your husband or older children. Tell them the big events of the week, ask what they have coming up (a school excursion, a football match, a work trip), and agree who handles which errand. Writing everyone's commitments on one shared page avoids the Sunday-night surprise of 'Mummy, I need cardboard for school tomorrow'. A shared Google Calendar works well for families who all have smartphones.

blocks.title: Plans for shift workers and traders
blocks.text: If your work hours change every week, as for nurses, market traders or drivers, do the weekly session as soon as you know your schedule. Plan your big rocks on days off first, and keep work days for small tasks only. A plan that respects your real hours is better than a perfect plan you cannot follow.

takeaways: Plan once a week for 30 minutes at a fixed time.
Place big rocks (important tasks) before small tasks.
Each day, choose a top three and do one before social media.
Leave buffer time and swap tasks when power or plans change.

activity.title: Plan next week
steps: Choose and diary your weekly planning time.
Run the six-step session for next week.
Write your top three each day for at least five days.
Mark each top-three task done or not done.
At the end of the week, note what broke the plan and how you adjusted.
activity.evidence: A photo of your weekly plan and five daily top-three lists with ticks.

lessons.title: Setting Realistic Goals and Timelines
objectives: Write a goal using the SMART checklist
Break a goal into milestones and weekly actions
Estimate realistic timelines with a safety margin
Track progress and adjust without giving up

blocks.text: Goals give your weekly plan a direction. Without them, big rocks are hard to choose. But vague goals such as 'save more' or 'grow my business' rarely happen. This lesson shows how to turn a wish into a goal with steps and dates.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.alt: A person reaching a target with a flag
blocks.caption: A clear goal broken into milestones gives you something specific to place in each week's plan.

blocks.text: The SMART checklist

head: Letter
Meaning
Question to ask
rows: What exactly will I do or achieve?
How will I know it is done? What number or result?
Is this possible with my money, time and skills?
Does it matter to me and my family right now?

blocks.text: For example, 'save more' becomes: 'Save 150,000 naira (approximately) for my son's next school fees by 1 September, by putting aside 15,000 naira every week.' Now you can check every week whether you are on track.
From goal to daily action

Big goals feel heavy. Break them down into layers. A **milestone** is a checkpoint along the way. A **weekly action** is something you can put in your weekly plan. A **daily action** is small enough to do in one sitting.

blocks.title: From vision to daily action
items: Vision: the life you want
Goal: SMART, with a date
Milestones: monthly checkpoints
Weekly actions
Daily actions
blocks.caption: Each layer is smaller and more concrete than the one above; you only ever act at the bottom.

blocks.title: Worked example: a goal broken down
blocks.context: For example, Esther wants to start selling zobo and chapman drinks from home in Benin City within three months. Prices below are illustrative.
steps: SMART goal: sell my first 50 bottles of zobo to paying customers by 30 June.
Milestone 1 (end of April): recipe tested three times, costs worked out per bottle.
Milestone 2 (end of May): 60 clean bottles and labels bought; food hygiene steps written down; price list ready.
Milestone 3 (mid June): first batch sold to 10 neighbours and church members; feedback collected.
Weekly actions in April: Week 1 buy ingredients and test recipe; Week 2 test again and adjust sugar; Week 3 calculate cost per bottle; Week 4 third test and taste panel with family.
Daily action for Monday: write the shopping list for the first test batch.
blocks.result: Esther's goal now lives inside her weekly plans. Each week has one or two small actions, and she can see on her calendar exactly where she is.

blocks.text: Realistic timelines

Most people underestimate how long things take, because they plan for the best case and forget interruptions, travel, power cuts and waiting for other people. A simple rule of thumb: estimate the time, then add half again. If you think sewing a dress will take 4 hours, plan 6. If you think a supplier will deliver in a week, plan for two. Over time, compare your estimates with the real times you recorded and adjust.

items: **Choose one or two goals at a time.** Five goals at once usually means none get enough time.
**Check money as well as time.** A goal that needs 200,000 naira you do not have needs a savings milestone first.
**Write down what you need from others.** If your goal depends on a husband, sister or supplier, agree it with them early.

blocks.text: Tracking and adjusting

In your weekly review, check each goal: on track, a little behind, or stuck. If you are behind, ask why. Was the timeline too short? Did something urgent take over? Do you need help or money? Adjusting a date is not failure. Abandoning the goal without asking why is what to avoid.

blocks.title: Goals for the whole family
blocks.text: Goals do not have to be only yours. A family goal, such as 'Everyone in bed by 10 pm on school nights' or 'Save for a family holiday in December', can be agreed together and tracked on the fridge.
Goals and money together

Many goals for women in business and home management are money goals: school fees, rent, equipment, stock, a family emergency fund. For these, divide the amount by the number of weeks left to find a weekly saving target. For example, 120,000 naira over 12 weeks is 10,000 naira a week. If that number is too high for your budget, either extend the date or reduce the goal. A savings group (ajo, esusu or adashe) or a separate savings account can help you keep the money aside, but only join groups run by people you know and trust, with clear written records.
Finally, celebrate milestones. When you reach one, mark it on your plan and tell someone who supports you. Small celebrations keep motivation alive over the weeks it takes to reach a big goal.

takeaways: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Break goals into milestones, weekly actions and daily actions.
Estimate time, then add half again for real life.
Review goals weekly and adjust dates rather than giving up.

activity.title: One SMART goal with steps
steps: Write one goal you care about for the next three months.
Rewrite it using the five SMART questions.
Set two or three monthly milestones.
List four weekly actions for the first month and add them to your weekly plans.
Track it in your weekly review for four weeks.
activity.evidence: Your written SMART goal with milestones and four weeks of progress notes.

lessons.title: The Art of Saying No: Protecting Your Plan Respectfully
objectives: Recognise when a yes will damage your plan or wellbeing
Use the pause before answering any request
Say no respectfully, including to elders and close family
Offer alternatives such as a smaller yes or a later date

blocks.text: Your plan will be tested by requests: a relative who needs you to cook for a party, a friend who wants you to follow her to the market, a church committee looking for volunteers, a customer who wants a dress by tomorrow. In many Nigerian families and communities, saying no can feel rude, especially to elders. This lesson is about saying no in a way that protects both your time and your relationships.

blocks.name: no-entry-sign
blocks.caption: A respectful no protects the time you set aside for your most important tasks.

blocks.text: Every yes is also a no

When you say yes to one thing, you say no to something else in your 168 hours. If you agree to spend Saturday cooking for a cousin's party, you are saying no to your market day, your rest or your sewing orders. Before agreeing, ask yourself: what will I give up for this?
The pause

The most powerful tool is not the word 'no'. It is the pause. Most requests do not need an answer immediately. Train yourself to say: **'Let me check my week and get back to you this evening.'** This gives you time to look at your plan and decide calmly, instead of agreeing out of habit or pressure.

If you decide to say yes, say a full yes. Agree the exact time you can give, write it in your plan, and arrive ready. Half-hearted yeses, where you agree but arrive late or leave early with complaints, often damage relationships more than a kind no.

blocks.title: Deciding on a request
items: Pause before answering
Check your plan
Ask: important to me?
Yes, smaller yes, or no
Reply kindly and clearly
blocks.caption: Pausing and checking your plan turns a pressured answer into a real decision.

blocks.text: Ways to say no kindly

head: Situation
What you could say
rows: A friend asks you to come along to the market on your work afternoon
'I would love to, but I have orders to finish today. Can we go together on Saturday?'
A relative asks you to cook for a large event
'I cannot cook for the whole event this time, but I can make one tray of jollof and bring it.'
A customer wants a rush job
'I cannot do it by tomorrow without rushing it. I can deliver on Friday, or by tomorrow with a rush fee.'
'Thank you for thinking of me. I already serve on one committee, and I want to do that one well.'
Request for money you do not have
'I am sorry, I cannot help with money this month. I am keeping to my family budget.'

blocks.text: Notice the pattern: a warm opening, a clear answer, a short reason if you want to give one, and often an alternative. You do not need to give long excuses. Long explanations invite argument.

blocks.title: Worked example: a smaller yes
blocks.context: For example, Patience's aunt calls on Thursday asking her to spend all of Saturday helping prepare food for a naming ceremony. Patience has planned Saturday for her tailoring orders, which are due on Monday.
steps: She pauses: 'Aunty, let me check how my week is and I will call you back tonight.'
She checks her plan: four orders due Monday need about 6 hours on Saturday.
She decides on a smaller yes: she can come for 2 hours on Saturday morning to help with the peppers and onions, then return to her sewing.
She calls back: 'Aunty, congratulations again. I have customer orders due Monday, so I cannot stay the whole day, but I will come from 7 to 9 in the morning to help with the preparation.'
Her aunt accepts and is grateful for the help.
blocks.result: Patience keeps the relationship warm, helps her family, and still delivers her orders on time.

blocks.title: Watch out for money scams that use urgency
blocks.text: Messages saying a relative is in trouble and needs money sent immediately, or that you must pay a fee to receive a prize, use urgency to stop you thinking. Pause, call the person directly on a number you already know, and never share your bank PIN or one-time password (OTP) with anyone.
When it is hard to say no

items: **Elders:** speak with respect, offer what you can, and if possible ask another family member to share the load.
**Husband or partner:** talk about the weekly plan together, so requests fit into it instead of competing with it.
**Guilt afterwards:** remind yourself that protecting your time is how you keep your promises to customers, children and yourself.

blocks.text: Saying no gets easier with practice. Start with low-risk requests, such as declining to join a new WhatsApp group or postponing a casual visit, and build confidence before the harder conversations. Many women find that people respect a clear and kind no more than a reluctant yes that is done late or with resentment.

takeaways: Every yes uses hours you planned for something else.
Pause: 'Let me check my week and get back to you.'
A kind no has a warm opening, a clear answer and often an alternative.
A smaller yes or a later date can protect both time and relationships.

activity.title: Practise the pause
steps: Write your own version of the pause sentence and learn it.
Write two kind no replies for requests you often receive.
For one week, use the pause for every non-urgent request.
Note each request, your answer, and how it affected your plan.
Reflect: which reply worked best, and why?
activity.evidence: Your written reply scripts and a one-week request log with your answers.

quiz.q: Ifeoma's list includes: servicing the generator next month, a customer order due in two hours, and forwarding a chain message. Which belongs in 'Schedule' (important, not urgent)?
quiz.explain: Servicing the generator matters but is not due today, so it should be given a time in the calendar before it becomes an emergency.

quiz.q: Why does scheduling quadrant 2 tasks reduce stress over time?
options: It means you never have to work in quadrant 1
Important tasks done early stop turning into emergencies later
It removes the need to delegate
It makes urgent tasks less important
quiz.explain: When important tasks are handled before they become urgent, fewer crises land in quadrant 1.

quiz.q: In a weekly planning session, what should be placed on the calendar first after fixed commitments?
options: Your three to five big rocks
quiz.explain: Big rocks (the most important tasks) go in first so small tasks fit around them, not the other way round.

quiz.q: Sade thinks building her online shop page will take 4 hours. Using the course rule of thumb, how much time should she plan?
quiz.explain: Estimate, then add half again: 4 + 2 = 6 hours.

quiz.q: Which goal is SMART?
options: Sell 30 bags of chin chin to new customers by 31 March
quiz.explain: It is specific, measurable (30 bags), achievable, relevant to a business, and has a date.

quiz.q: A friend asks Uche to help at her shop all day on Saturday, the day Uche planned for her own orders. What is the best first response?
options: Say 'Let me check my week and get back to you this evening'
Give a long list of reasons
quiz.explain: Pausing gives time to check the plan and choose a yes, a smaller yes or a kind no.

modules.title: Home Management Systems
modules.overview: Good systems mean the home runs without you holding every detail in your head. In this module you design daily and weekly routines, share chores fairly across the household, plan meals and a household budget together, and manage the family calendar of school, events and community commitments.

lessons.title: Designing Daily and Weekly Home Routines
objectives: Build a short morning and evening routine for your home
Create a weekly cleaning and laundry schedule
Plan around power supply and water storage
Keep routines simple enough to follow on busy days

blocks.text: A **routine** is a set of tasks done in the same order at roughly the same time. Routines save time because you stop deciding what to do next; the steps become automatic. They also make it easier for others in the home to help, because everyone knows what happens when. This lesson helps you design routines for your real home, including power cuts and water.

blocks.name: schedule-cleanup
blocks.alt: A person organising a schedule board
blocks.caption: A written routine turns many small daily decisions into one familiar sequence.

blocks.text: The morning routine

Mornings are often the most rushed part of the day, especially on school days. Most of a calm morning is actually prepared the night before. Keep your morning list short, five to seven steps, and put it in order.

items: Wake up at a fixed time, ideally 20 to 30 minutes before the children.
Personal time: prayer, a glass of water, a look at your top three tasks.
Start breakfast (prepared or partly prepared the night before).
Children wash and dress; uniforms and bags were set out last night.
Quick tidy: beds made, breakfast dishes soaked or washed.
Leave on time with everything checked: keys, phone, lunch packs.

blocks.text: The evening reset

The evening reset prepares tomorrow and stops mess from building up. Even 20 to 30 minutes makes a big difference. A good evening reset includes: kitchen cleared and pots washed, uniforms and bags ready, a quick check of tomorrow's plan, phones charging, and a 10-minute tidy of the main room with everyone helping.

blocks.title: A sample school-day routine
items: 5:30 am: wake, plan, pray
6:00 am: breakfast and dressing
7:00 am: school run
6:00 pm: dinner and homework
8:30 pm: evening reset
10:00 pm: bed
blocks.caption: Fixed anchor times hold the day together; the tasks between them can move when needed.

blocks.text: A weekly cleaning and laundry schedule
Instead of cleaning everything on Saturday, spread tasks across the week. Each day has one main task that takes 20 to 40 minutes. Saturday is then lighter and leaves time for rest and family.

head: Day
Main home task
Notes
rows: Wash early when water is available
Wear gloves; never mix bleach with other cleaners
Plan for a time when power is usually on
Kitchen deep clean: fridge, cooker, cupboards
Sweep and mop all rooms, dust surfaces

blocks.title: Cleaning products safely
blocks.text: Never mix bleach (such as Hypo) with other cleaning products, especially those containing ammonia or acids, because dangerous gases can form. Open windows when cleaning, wear gloves, and store all chemicals high up, in their original labelled containers, away from children and food.
Planning around power and water

items: Notice the usual times your power comes on (or note your generator or solar hours) and plan ironing, blending and washing machine use for those times.
Keep phones, power banks and rechargeable lamps charged whenever power is on.
Fill and cover water containers at a fixed time when supply is available. Clean storage drums and buckets regularly and keep them covered to prevent contamination and mosquito breeding.
Keep a simple no-power task list: folding, sorting, planning, market.

blocks.title: Worked example: rebuilding a routine
blocks.context: For example, Blessing lives in Owerri with her husband and three children. Mornings were chaos and Saturdays were spent entirely on cleaning.
steps: She writes a six-step morning routine and sticks it on the bedroom door.
She adds a 25-minute evening reset at 8:30 pm: everyone tidies for 10 minutes, she prepares breakfast ingredients, the children lay out uniforms.
She spreads cleaning across the week with the table above, one 30-minute task per day.
She moves ironing to Wednesday evenings, when power has usually been steady in her area.
After three weeks: the family leaves on time on most mornings and Saturday cleaning has dropped from about 6 hours to about 1 hour.
blocks.result: Blessing gains most of her Saturday back for rest, family and her small online business.

blocks.text: Start with one routine, usually the evening reset, because it makes the morning easier too. Once it feels natural after two or three weeks, add the next.
Monthly and occasional tasks

Some tasks come round less often: defrosting the freezer, washing curtains, cleaning the water tank or drums, checking the gas cylinder hose, fumigating, servicing the generator. Write them on a monthly list and put one or two into each week's plan so they never pile up. A good habit is to give the first Saturday of each month a short 'home check' of 30 minutes for these jobs.

On very busy days, such as when a child is sick or a big order is due, shrink routines to the minimum: food cooked, dishes washed, children ready for school. Skipping the extras for one day is fine; the routine is there to serve you.

takeaways: Routines save decisions and make it easy for others to help.
A calm morning is prepared the night before.
Spread cleaning across the week: one main task per day.
Plan power-dependent tasks for your usual supply times and keep water stored safely.

activity.title: Write your routines
steps: Write a morning routine of five to seven steps for your home.
Write an evening reset of four to six steps.
Fill in a weekly cleaning and laundry table for your household.
Post the routines where everyone can see them.
Follow them for one week and note what to change.
activity.evidence: Photos of your posted routines and weekly schedule, plus a note of changes after one week.

lessons.title: Sharing the Load: Chores, Children and Household Help
objectives: List all the work your household needs, including invisible tasks
Match chores to each family member's age and ability
Hold a short family meeting to agree responsibilities
Work fairly and clearly with a house help if you have one

blocks.text: In many homes, one woman carries most of the housework, the childcare and the mental load of remembering everything. That is not a time management problem you can solve by working faster. It is solved by sharing. This lesson gives you a practical method to share chores across the household, in a way that suits your family and culture.

blocks.name: working-together
blocks.alt: Several people working together on a shared task
blocks.caption: When everyone in the home has a clear part, the work stops resting on one person.

blocks.text: Step 1: Make the invisible work visible

Write a list of every task the home needs, daily, weekly and monthly. Include the **mental load**: remembering school fees deadlines, noticing when the gas is low, planning meals, remembering birthdays, booking the plumber. These tasks take time and energy even though nobody sees them. Seeing the full list often surprises the rest of the family.
Step 2: Match tasks to ability

Children can do more than we often expect, and learning chores builds skills they will need as adults. Always think about safety first: young children should be kept away from hot pots, sharp knives, cleaning chemicals and electrical sockets.

head: Age (approximate)
Suitable tasks with supervision
Keep away from
rows: Pick up toys, put clothes in the laundry basket, wipe small spills
Make own bed, set and clear the table, sweep, fold small clothes, water plants
Wash dishes, sweep and mop, simple cooking with an adult nearby, wash own socks and underwear
Cook simple meals, iron, do laundry, short errands, help younger siblings
Tasks that clash with study time
Equal share of cooking, cleaning, errands, school runs and planning

blocks.text: Step 3: Hold a family meeting

Choose a calm time, such as after Sunday lunch, and keep it to 20 minutes. Explain why: 'I want us all to have more rest and time together.' Show the list. Let each person choose some tasks first; people do chores better when they had a say. Fill the gaps fairly. Write the result on a chore chart and post it.

blocks.title: The chore-sharing cycle
items: List all tasks
Match to ability
Agree at family meeting
Post the chore chart
Review monthly
blocks.caption: Sharing is not a one-off decision; review the chart every month as children grow and schedules change.

blocks.title: Worked example: a family chore chart
blocks.context: For example, Fatima in Ilorin has a husband who works shifts, a 12-year-old son and an 8-year-old daughter. She has been doing almost everything.
steps: She lists 28 regular tasks, including 'remember to buy gas' and 'check homework'.
At a Sunday family meeting, her son chooses washing dishes after dinner and sweeping the compound; her daughter chooses setting the table and folding clothes.
Her husband takes the Saturday market run, paying the electricity bill and the school run on his days off.
She posts a chart with names, tasks and days, with a tick box for each.
After a month they review: her daughter swaps folding for watering plants, and the son adds ironing his own uniform.
blocks.result: Fatima's daily housework drops by about 1.5 hours, and the children are proud of their ticks. The monthly review keeps it fair.

blocks.text: Making it stick

items: **Teach once, properly.** Show how to do the task, do it together once, then let them try.
**Accept good enough.** If the floor is swept but not perfectly, thank them. Redoing it teaches them it does not matter.
**Praise effort, specifically:** 'Thank you for washing the pots so well tonight.'
**Link to privileges, not punishment,** where it suits your family, for example screen time after chores are done.

blocks.text: Working with a house help

If you employ a house help, treat it as a job with clear terms. Agree the duties, working hours, rest day, pay and payment date in advance, ideally written down. Pay on time. Provide proper food, a safe place to sleep if they live in, and protective gloves for cleaning. Never employ a child as a house help instead of sending them to school; a young person living with you should be in school, and chores should be shared fairly as with your own children.

blocks.title: Talking with your husband
blocks.text: In some homes, men sharing housework is new. Start with tasks that fit his schedule and interests, such as errands, school runs, paying bills or weekend cooking, and focus on the shared goal: a calmer home and more family time.

If a family member does not do an agreed task, talk about it privately and calmly at the next review instead of quietly doing it yourself. Quietly taking it back teaches everyone that the chart is optional.

Remember the mental load too. Hand over whole tasks, not just the doing. 'You are in charge of buying gas: check the level every Friday and buy when it is low' removes the remembering from you, while 'Please buy gas when I tell you' does not.

takeaways: List all household tasks, including the invisible mental load.
Match chores to age and ability, keeping children away from hazards.
Agree tasks at a short family meeting and post a chore chart.
Treat a house help fairly: clear duties, hours, rest and pay on time.

activity.title: Create your chore chart
steps: List every regular household task, including mental-load tasks.
Mark which tasks each person could do safely.
Hold a 20-minute family meeting to agree responsibilities.
Make and post a chore chart with names, tasks, days and tick boxes.
Review it after four weeks and adjust.
activity.evidence: A photo of your posted chore chart and a short note from the four-week review.

lessons.title: Meal Planning and Household Budgeting
objectives: Plan a weekly menu and build a market list from it
Batch cook and store food safely using the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Build a simple monthly household budget
Track spending with an envelope or notebook method

blocks.text: Food and money are linked: food is usually one of the largest parts of a household's spending, and 'What are we eating today?' is asked every day. A weekly meal plan saves time, money and stress, and a simple budget makes sure the money lasts to the end of the month.

blocks.name: groceries
blocks.alt: A woman carrying a bag of groceries
blocks.caption: A menu and a market list built from it mean fewer trips and less money spent on impulse.

blocks.text: Part 1: Plan the week's meals

items: Check what you already have: rice, beans, garri, yam, oil, frozen fish, pepper mix.
Check your week's plan: busy days need quick meals or leftovers.
Choose meals for each day using a pattern, for example: rice-based on Monday, beans on Tuesday, swallow with soup on Wednesday, yam or plantain on Thursday.
Plan to cook bases in bulk: a big pot of stew and one soup can serve several meals.
Write the market list from the menu, grouped by where you buy (market, supermarket, butcher).

blocks.text: Aim for variety across the week: a starchy food (rice, yam, garri, bread), a protein (beans, eggs, fish, meat, chicken), and vegetables (ugu, spinach, okra, tomatoes) or fruit each day. Beans, eggs and fish are often cheaper sources of protein than meat.

blocks.title: From menu to table
items: Check stock at home
Write weekly menu
Make market list
One market trip
Batch cook and store
blocks.caption: Each step feeds the next; skipping the menu is what causes daily extra trips and waste.

blocks.text: Batch cooking and safe storage

Batch cooking means cooking large amounts once and storing portions. Follow the World Health Organization's **Five Keys to Safer Food**: keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials. In practice:

items: Wash hands before cooking and after touching raw meat or fish.
Use separate boards or wash them well between raw meat and ready-to-eat food.
Cool cooked food quickly and put it in the fridge or freezer within 2 hours. Do not leave stew out overnight at room temperature.
Store in clean, covered containers in portions for one meal, so you only reheat what you need.
Reheat until steaming hot all the way through, and reheat only once.
During long power cuts, keep the freezer closed. If frozen food has fully thawed and warmed, cook it straight away or throw it away.

blocks.text: Part 2: The household budget

A **budget** is a plan for your money before you spend it. Write your monthly income from all sources (salary, business profit, regular support from family). Then list spending in three groups: **needs** (rent, food, school fees, transport, electricity, water, gas, health), **wants** (eating out, new clothes beyond the basics, data for entertainment), and **savings** (emergency fund, school fees fund, business). A common rule of thumb is 50% needs, 30% wants and 20% savings, but in many Nigerian households needs take more than half. That is fine: the aim is to plan, and to save something regularly, even 5% to start.

blocks.title: Worked example: a monthly budget
blocks.context: For example, Ruth and her husband in Jos bring in about 400,000 naira a month together. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Needs: rent saved monthly 60,000; food 140,000; school fees saved monthly 40,000; transport 35,000; electricity, water and gas 30,000; health and toiletries 15,000. Total needs 320,000 (80%).
Savings: emergency fund 30,000 and business stock 10,000. Total 40,000 (10%).
Wants: data for entertainment, outings, gifts 40,000 (10%).
Check: 320,000 + 40,000 + 40,000 = 400,000. Every naira has a job.
Meal planning cuts their food spending from about 160,000 to 140,000 by reducing waste and extra trips; the 20,000 saved goes to the emergency fund.
blocks.result: Ruth's family knows exactly where the money goes, saves 10% every month, and can see that meal planning pays for their emergency fund.

blocks.text: Tracking spending

A budget only works if you check it. Two simple methods: the **envelope method** (put cash for each category, such as food or transport, into labelled envelopes; when an envelope is empty, that category is finished for the month) and the **notebook method** (write every expense with the date and category, and add up weekly). If you pay mostly by transfer, many banking apps such as Opay, Moniepoint or your bank's app show your transaction history, which you can check each week.

blocks.title: Protect your money
blocks.text: Never share your PIN, password or OTP with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank. Banks do not ask for these by phone or message.

Buying some staples in bulk, such as a bag of rice, a paint bucket of garri or a gallon of oil, can lower the cost per meal, but only if you have the cash without cutting other needs and somewhere dry and pest-free to store them. Some women share a bag with a neighbour or join a food cooperative to get bulk prices on a smaller budget.

takeaways: Plan meals weekly from what you have, then write one market list.
Batch cook, cool quickly, store covered and reheat until steaming hot.
Budget income into needs, wants and savings; give every naira a job.
Track spending weekly with envelopes, a notebook or your bank app.

activity.title: One week of meals and one month of money
steps: Write a seven-day menu for your household.
Turn it into a market list and do one main market trip.
Batch cook at least one stew or soup and store it in portions.
Write a monthly budget with needs, wants and savings that adds up to your income.
Track every expense for one week.
activity.evidence: Photos of your menu, market list and stored portions, plus your written budget and one-week spending record.

lessons.title: Managing School, Family and Community Commitments
objectives: Set up one family calendar for school, family and community events
Prepare early for predictable busy periods such as school resumption
Plan for events, celebrations and contributions in time and money
Use reminders so commitments do not surprise you

blocks.text: Beyond daily routines, every household has a stream of commitments: school terms, PTA meetings, open days, birthdays, weddings and naming ceremonies, church or mosque activities, cooperative meetings, visits to the village. Many of them are known weeks or months ahead, yet still arrive as surprises. This lesson shows you how to see them coming.

blocks.name: school-satchel
blocks.caption: School terms follow a known pattern, so resumption costs and tasks can be planned long before the first day.

blocks.text: One family calendar

Choose one place where every commitment is written: a large wall calendar in the kitchen, or a shared Google Calendar if all the adults have smartphones. Use one colour or symbol per person. The rule is simple: if it is not on the calendar, it is not planned.

items: School: term start and end dates, mid-term breaks, exams, PTA meetings, open days, fees deadlines.
Family: birthdays, anniversaries, visits, medical appointments, vaccinations.
Community: weddings, burials, naming ceremonies, church or mosque programmes, cooperative or ajo meetings.
Money dates: rent due, school fees, levies, contributions.

blocks.text: Prepare early for predictable peaks
Some periods are always busy: school resumption, festive seasons such as Christmas, Sallah and Easter, and the end of the year. Make a checklist for each and start four to six weeks before.

blocks.title: School resumption checklist
items: Fees saved or paid
Uniforms and shoes checked
Books and stationery bought
Lunch box and bottle ready
Routines restarted a week early
blocks.caption: Starting this list a month before resumption spreads both the cost and the work.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning the September resumption
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Lagos has three children in primary and secondary school. Last year she spent the weekend before resumption rushing between markets.
steps: In early July, she writes the resumption date on the family calendar and sets a reminder for 1 August.
On 1 August, she checks uniforms and shoes with each child and lists what is needed.
She divides the expected cost by 5 weeks and saves a fixed amount weekly in a separate account.
In mid August, she buys books and stationery on a weekday, when the market is quieter.
One week before resumption, the children return to school-day bedtimes and the morning routine.
blocks.result: Resumption morning is calm, everything is ready, and the cost was spread across five weeks instead of landing in one.

blocks.text: Events, celebrations and contributions
Social events are an important part of family and community life, and they cost time and money: aso ebi fabric, sewing, transport, gifts, contributions. Plan them like any other commitment.

head: Question
Why it helps
rows: Is attendance important to me or my family?
Helps you choose which events to attend fully, briefly or not at all
What will it cost in total, including aso ebi, tailoring, transport and gift?
Avoids surprise spending that breaks the budget
How much time, including travel and preparation?
Lets you plan orders and chores around it
Can I contribute in another way?
A smaller gift, helping for two hours, or attending only the main ceremony

blocks.text: Consider keeping a small monthly 'events' line in your budget, so contributions come from planned money rather than from food or school fees.
School communication

Many schools now send notices by WhatsApp or text. When a notice arrives, act on it at once: put the date on the calendar, add any cost to your budget, and note any item a child must bring. This takes two minutes (remember the two-minute rule) and prevents the late-night 'I need this tomorrow' crisis. Ask your children to give you paper notices the same day, in a fixed place such as a tray by the door.

blocks.title: Use repeating reminders
blocks.text: In Google Calendar or your phone's calendar, set yearly reminders for birthdays and term dates, and monthly reminders for rent and contributions. Set the reminder one or two weeks before, not on the day.
Community roles and volunteering
Agree with your husband or co-parent who attends which school event. Taking turns at PTA meetings and open days shares the time and keeps both parents connected with the school and the teachers.

Many women serve in church or mosque groups, women's associations, cooperatives and school PTAs. These roles are valuable, but they can quietly take many hours a week. Once a year, list every role you hold, the hours each takes per month, and what it gives you and your family. Keep the ones that matter most, and hand over or step back from the rest at the end of the term, giving the group enough notice to find someone new.

For family visits and travel, such as going to the village at Christmas, plan the trip on the calendar early, book transport ahead where you can, and agree who looks after the house, the shop or customers while you are away. Tell regular customers your closing and reopening dates in advance through a WhatsApp status or broadcast.

takeaways: Keep one family calendar; if it is not on it, it is not planned.
Start checklists four to six weeks before predictable busy periods.
Plan events in time and money, and choose how fully to take part.
Act on school notices immediately and use reminders before key dates.

activity.title: Build your family calendar
steps: Set up a wall or shared phone calendar for the household.
Add all known school dates, birthdays and money dates for the next three months.
Add any known community events and estimate their cost.
Write a checklist for the next predictable busy period.
Set reminders one to two weeks before each key date.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your filled family calendar and your checklist for the next busy period.

quiz.q: Ngozi's mornings are always rushed. According to the course, where is most of a calm morning actually prepared?
options: In the evening reset the night before
quiz.explain: Setting out uniforms, preparing breakfast ingredients and checking tomorrow's plan in the evening makes mornings calmer.

quiz.q: Which chore is suitable for a 7-year-old with supervision?
quiz.explain: Setting the table is safe and achievable; hot oil, gas cylinders and bleach are hazards for young children.

quiz.q: Lami cooked a big pot of stew at 2 pm. What is the safe way to store it?
options: Leave it on the cooker until tomorrow
Cool it quickly and refrigerate or freeze it in covered portions within 2 hours
Cover it and leave it in the kitchen for the week
quiz.explain: WHO guidance is to keep food at safe temperatures: cool and refrigerate cooked food promptly, store it covered, and reheat until steaming hot.

quiz.q: A household earns 300,000 naira a month. Needs cost 240,000 and wants 30,000. How much is left for savings if every naira has a job?
quiz.explain: 300,000 minus 240,000 minus 30,000 leaves 30,000 naira for savings.

quiz.q: Which method stops overspending by keeping cash for each category in a labelled container?
quiz.explain: In the envelope method, each category has its own cash; when the envelope is empty, that category is finished for the month.

quiz.q: A school WhatsApp message announces a cultural day in two weeks, with a costume needed. What should Halima do first?
options: Put it on the family calendar, add the cost to the budget and note the costume
quiz.explain: Acting on notices immediately, using the two-minute rule, prevents last-minute crises.

modules.title: Balance, Boundaries and Wellbeing
modules.overview: Plans fail when the person running them is exhausted. This module covers rest and recovery, setting and keeping boundaries, balancing a small business or job with home and family, and building a monthly and quarterly review that keeps your systems working for years.

lessons.title: Rest, Recovery and the Myth of Busyness
objectives: Explain why rest is part of productivity, not the opposite of it
Plan for enough sleep and short breaks in your day
Use focused work periods with breaks, such as the Pomodoro technique
Recognise the signs of burnout and know when to seek help

blocks.text: Many women are praised for never resting: first up, last to bed, always on their feet. But a tired mind makes more mistakes, takes longer over tasks and gets irritable more easily. Rest is not laziness. It is maintenance, like servicing a generator so it keeps running.

blocks.name: relaxing-at-home
blocks.alt: A woman relaxing on a sofa at home
blocks.caption: Planned rest is part of a working system, not a reward you earn only when everything is done.

blocks.text: Sleep first

Health authorities such as the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advise that most adults need **7 or more hours of sleep** a night. Regularly sleeping less is linked with poorer concentration and health. Protect sleep the way you protect a customer delivery.

items: Choose a fixed bedtime and wake time, even at weekends where possible.
Use your phone's Bedtime mode (Android) or Sleep Focus (iPhone) to silence notifications at night.
Stop screens 30 minutes before bed and keep the phone away from the pillow.
Keep the room as dark and cool as you can; a fan or open window helps in the heat, with a mosquito net.
Avoid heavy meals and strong coffee or tea late in the evening.

blocks.text: Short breaks during the day

Long stretches of work without a pause wear down attention. Short breaks restore it. The **Pomodoro technique**, developed by Francesco Cirillo, is a simple method: work on one task for **25 minutes**, then take a **5-minute break**. After four rounds, take a longer break of 15 to 30 minutes. You can use your phone's timer or a kitchen timer.

blocks.title: The Pomodoro cycle
items: Choose one task
Work 25 minutes
Break 5 minutes
Repeat four times
Long break 15 to 30 minutes
blocks.caption: Short, regular breaks keep focus steady across a long working day.

blocks.text: A good break means actually stepping away: stretch, drink water, step outside, talk with someone. Scrolling social media during a break often leaves the mind just as busy.

blocks.title: Worked example: adding rest without losing output
blocks.context: For example, Mercy makes and sells bead jewellery in Calabar. She often worked from 6 am to midnight and was making mistakes in her orders.
steps: She sets a bedtime of 11 pm and wake time of 6 am, giving 7 hours.
She works on beading in Pomodoro rounds: 25 minutes focused, 5 minutes stretching or water.
She takes a 30-minute lunch break away from her worktable.
She keeps Sunday afternoon free of orders for rest and family.
After three weeks she counts: errors in orders dropped from about 4 a week to 1, and she still completes the same number of pieces.
blocks.result: Mercy works fewer hours, makes fewer mistakes and feels less irritable with her children, with no drop in sales.

blocks.text: Types of rest

head: Type of rest
What it looks like
rows: Sleep, a nap, sitting down with feet up, gentle stretching
A walk without the phone, a short quiet time, prayer or reflection
Time with people who encourage you, not only people who need things from you
Music, gardening, cooking for pleasure, a hobby

blocks.text: The myth of busyness

Busyness can feel like proof that you are working hard or are a good mother. But results matter more than activity. A woman who rests well and finishes her top three tasks has done better than one who rushed all day and finished none. In your weekly review, measure what you finished, not how tired you are.
Building rest into your week
