Rest that is not planned rarely happens, because there is always one more task. Put rest into your weekly plan as a real appointment. A useful pattern is a short daily pause (15 to 30 minutes after lunch or when the children come home), one longer weekly rest (a half-day, such as Sunday afternoon) and a yearly break (a few days around a holiday when the business closes). Tell your family when your rest times are, and ask them to protect them as you protect theirs.

Mothers of babies and small children often cannot get unbroken sleep. In that season, take rest where you can: sleep when the baby sleeps on at least some days, accept offers of help with cooking or older children, and lower your expectations for the house. The season passes.

blocks.title: Signs of burnout
blocks.text: The World Health Organization describes burnout as a result of chronic workplace stress that has not been managed, with feelings of exhaustion, mental distance or negativity about one's work, and reduced effectiveness. If you feel this way for weeks, feel hopeless, or cannot cope, talk to someone you trust and see a doctor or health worker. Asking for help is a strong and sensible step.

Track rest in your weekly review just as you track tasks. If your energy scores stay low for several weeks even with better sleep, look again at your workload and the chores you could share, and consider a health check.

takeaways: Rest is maintenance that keeps you productive.
Most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep; protect it with a fixed bedtime.
Use focused rounds with short breaks, such as 25 minutes on, 5 minutes off.
Know the signs of burnout and seek help early.

activity.title: A rest plan for two weeks
steps: Set a fixed bedtime and wake time that give you at least 7 hours.
Switch on Bedtime mode or Sleep Focus on your phone.
Use Pomodoro rounds for your main work for at least five days.
Plan one half-day of rest each week and write it in your plan.
Record your sleep hours and energy level (1 to 5) daily for two weeks.
activity.evidence: Your two-week sleep and energy record and a screenshot of your Bedtime or Sleep Focus setting.

lessons.title: Setting and Keeping Healthy Boundaries
objectives: Identify where you need boundaries: time, phone, money, space and energy
State a boundary clearly and kindly
Use tools such as WhatsApp Business away messages to support boundaries
Keep a boundary when it is tested

blocks.text: A **boundary** is a clear limit you set about what you will and will not do, and when. In Module 2 you learned to say no to single requests. Boundaries go further: they are standing rules that stop the same requests from coming again and again. They protect your plan, your rest and your relationships.

blocks.name: mindfulness
blocks.alt: A woman sitting calmly with her eyes closed
blocks.caption: Clear boundaries protect the calm and energy you need for the people and work that matter most.

blocks.text: Five kinds of boundary

head: Boundary
Example
rows: 'I do not take orders after 8 pm.' 'Saturday mornings are for family.'
'I reply to non-urgent messages at 12 noon and 6 pm.' 'No phones at the dinner table.'
'I do not lend money I cannot afford to lose.' 'Customers pay a deposit before I start.'
'My sewing corner is not a place to keep other things.' 'Please call before visiting.'
'I attend one evening event a week, not every one.'

blocks.text: How to set a boundary

items: **Notice the pressure point.** Where do you feel resentful, rushed or drained again and again? That is often where a boundary is missing.
**Decide the rule.** Make it specific: not 'I need more time' but 'No customer calls after 8 pm'.
**Say it once, clearly and kindly.** 'From next week, I will take orders between 8 am and 7 pm.'
**Support it with tools.** Set phone settings, away messages or a sign on the shop door.
**Keep it.** The first few times are the hardest. Respond calmly and repeat it.

blocks.title: Without and with a boundary
items: Without a boundary
With a clear boundary
right: Customers know when to expect replies
blocks.caption: A boundary is not unkind; it makes you more reliable to the people who depend on you.

blocks.text: Tools that help

items: **WhatsApp Business:** set business hours on your profile, an **away message** that replies automatically outside those hours, and **quick replies** for common questions such as prices and delivery.
**Do Not Disturb or Focus modes:** allow calls only from chosen contacts, such as family and your children's school.
**A deposit policy:** write it in your catalogue or status so customers know before ordering.
**A visible notice:** a small sign in your shop or on your gate with opening hours.

blocks.title: Worked example: a business-hours boundary
blocks.context: For example, Tolu sells ready-made clothes on WhatsApp from Abeokuta. Customers message at all hours, and she answers until past midnight.
steps: She decides: business hours 8 am to 7 pm, Monday to Saturday.
In WhatsApp Business she sets her business hours and an away message: 'Thank you for your message. Our hours are 8 am to 7 pm, Monday to Saturday. We will reply first thing tomorrow.'
She posts a status telling customers about the new hours.
One regular customer calls at 10 pm. Tolu does not answer, and replies at 8 am: 'Good morning, sorry I missed your call last night. How can I help?'
After a month, most customers message within hours; sales are the same, and she sleeps before midnight.
blocks.result: Tolu's boundary protects her evenings without losing customers, because the away message tells them exactly when she will reply.

blocks.text: When a boundary is tested

People may push back at first, especially if they are used to you always saying yes. Stay calm and repeat the boundary without long explanations: 'I understand. As I said, I take orders until 7 pm. I will be happy to help tomorrow morning.' If you make an exception for a true emergency, say so: 'This once, because it is urgent.' Otherwise, exceptions quickly become the new rule.

With family, boundaries often work best when framed around a shared benefit: 'If I finish my orders by 7, I can sit with you all in the evening.' People accept limits more easily when they can see what the limit gives them too.

blocks.title: Boundaries and your safety
blocks.text: If someone reacts to your boundaries with threats, intimidation or violence, your safety comes first. Speak to someone you trust and seek help from local support services, a community or faith leader you trust, or the police.

Boundaries also apply to yourself. 'I stop work at 9 pm even if I feel I could do more' is a boundary that protects your sleep. Self-boundaries are often the hardest to keep, so write them where you can see them and track them in your weekly review.

Review your boundaries every few months. As your business grows or your children get older, some boundaries need to change. A boundary that made sense with a newborn may be too strict when your children are at school, and a business that has grown may need stricter order cut-offs.

takeaways: Boundaries are standing rules about your time, phone, money, space and energy.
Make them specific, say them once kindly, and support them with tools.
WhatsApp Business hours, away messages and quick replies protect your evenings.
Repeat the boundary calmly when it is tested; true emergencies are the only exceptions.

activity.title: Set one boundary
steps: Write down the place in your life where you most often feel drained or resentful.
Turn it into one specific boundary sentence.
Tell the people affected, once, clearly and kindly.
Set up one tool that supports it, such as an away message or Focus mode.
Keep a note of each time it is tested and how you responded, for two weeks.
activity.evidence: Your written boundary, a screenshot of the supporting tool, and your two-week notes.

lessons.title: Balancing a Small Business or Job with Home and Family
objectives: Separate business time and money from household time and money
Plan work around the family's daily rhythm
Use batching and simple tools to run a home-based business efficiently
Arrange back-up childcare and support for busy periods

blocks.text: Many women in our network combine several roles: mother, wife, daughter, community member, and earner, whether through a job, a shop, a home-based business or selling online. When all these roles share the same hours and the same space, they blur together. This lesson gives practical ways to keep them balanced.

blocks.name: working-at-home
blocks.alt: A woman working on a laptop at home
blocks.caption: Working from home works best when business time and family time each have their own clear place in the day.

blocks.text: Separate business money and household money

Mixing business and home money is one of the most common reasons small businesses struggle. When stock money pays for groceries, you cannot see whether the business is making a profit, and you may not have money to restock.

items: Open a **separate account** for the business. Many banks and mobile money providers such as Opay, Moniepoint and Palmpay offer accounts you can open on a phone.
Pay yourself a **fixed amount** from the business into your household budget each week or month, rather than taking money whenever you need it.
Record every business sale and expense in a notebook or simple app.
Keep money for restocking aside before you pay yourself.

blocks.text: A simple test of whether your business is healthy: after paying for stock, transport, packaging and your fixed pay, is there still money left in the business account at the end of the month? If not, look at your prices and costs before taking on more orders.

blocks.title: Business money vs household money
items: Business account
Household budget
blocks.caption: Money moves from business to home only as a planned, fixed amount, so both stay healthy.

blocks.text: Fit work around the family rhythm

Look at your family's day and find the natural work windows: early morning before others wake, school hours, nap time for small children, evening after bedtime. Put your most demanding business work (production, accounts, important calls) in the quietest windows. Use busy family times for tasks that tolerate interruptions, such as replying to simple messages or packing orders.

blocks.title: Worked example: a home baker's week
blocks.context: For example, Zainab bakes cakes and meat pies at home in Abuja and has two children aged 4 and 9. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Work windows: 8:30 am to 1:00 pm while both children are at school or nursery, and 8:30 to 10:00 pm after bedtime.
Batching: she takes orders until Wednesday, buys all ingredients on Thursday, bakes on Friday and delivers on Saturday morning.
Messages: WhatsApp Business quick replies for prices and an away message after 7 pm.
Money: customers pay a 50% deposit by transfer to her business account; each Saturday she moves a fixed 25,000 naira to her household budget.
Back-up: her sister collects the children from school on Fridays, her main baking day, in exchange for a cake for her family each month.
blocks.result: Zainab's baking fits into planned windows, she knows her weekly profit, and the children are cared for on her busiest day.

blocks.text: Batching for business

Batching (Module 1) is especially powerful in business. Set an order cut-off day, buy supplies in one trip, produce in one session, and deliver on set days or by area. Post your product catalogue in WhatsApp Business so customers can see items and prices without asking you one by one. Fewer separate trips and fewer interruptions means more output in fewer hours.
Support for busy periods

items: **Childcare swaps:** take turns with a trusted neighbour, sister or friend to watch each other's children.
**Seasonal help:** hire short-term help for peak seasons such as December or Sallah, with agreed tasks and pay.
**Simplify home tasks in peak weeks:** batch-cooked meals, a lighter cleaning list, more chores shared by the family.
**Tell the family in advance:** 'This is a busy order week; I need everyone's help with the evening reset.'

blocks.title: Name your work hours aloud
blocks.text: Children and relatives respect work time more when they know it exists. Say: 'From 9 to 12 Mummy is working. After 12 we will have lunch together.' A small sign or a closed door helps younger children understand.
If you have an employer

If you work for an employer, the same ideas apply in a different way. Plan home tasks around your fixed office hours, use your commute or lunch break for planning and quick personal admin if it is safe and allowed, and prepare the evening before so mornings are not a race. If you have a side business as well, check your employment terms, keep it entirely outside working hours, and never use your employer's time, phone or equipment for it.

Guilt is common when you try to balance several roles: guilt about not being with the children, guilt about not answering a customer quickly. A useful question is: did I keep my most important promises this week? If yes, you are doing well, even if some things waited.

takeaways: Keep business and household money separate and pay yourself a fixed amount.
Put demanding work in the quietest family windows.
Batch business tasks with order cut-offs and set production and delivery days.
Arrange back-up childcare and tell the family about busy weeks in advance.

activity.title: Your work-home map
steps: Draw your family's typical day and mark your natural work windows.
Assign your main business or job tasks to those windows.
Set up or plan a separate business account and decide your fixed weekly pay.
Choose an order cut-off, production day and delivery day if you sell products.
Arrange one back-up childcare or support option for your busiest day.
activity.evidence: Your work-home map, your business-to-home pay decision, and a note of your support arrangement.

lessons.title: Building a Sustainable Life: Monthly and Quarterly Reviews
objectives: Run a monthly review across the main areas of your life
Use a quarterly reset to choose new goals and drop old commitments
Adjust your systems for different seasons of life
Bring together your plans, routines, budget and boundaries in one personal manual

blocks.text: Over this course you have built many tools: a time audit, the Eisenhower matrix, a weekly plan, goals, routines, a chore chart, a meal plan and budget, a family calendar, a rest plan and boundaries. This final lesson shows you how to keep them working for months and years, through reviews that let your systems change as your life changes.

blocks.name: personal-goals
blocks.alt: A woman reviewing her personal goals on a board
blocks.caption: Regular reviews keep your plans matched to the life you actually want.

blocks.text: The monthly review (45 minutes)
On the first weekend of each month, look back at the last month and score each area of life from 1 (very poor) to 5 (very good). Then choose one small improvement for the area with the lowest score.

head: Area
Questions to ask
rows: Did I sleep 7 or more hours most nights? Did I take my rest days?
Did we have time together? Is the chore chart working?
Did we keep to the budget? Did we save?
Did I meet my goals? Is the business making a profit?
Are routines working? Is the house manageable?
Did I make time for what feeds my spirit and mind?

blocks.title: Your planning rhythm
items: Daily top three
Weekly plan and review
Monthly life review
Quarterly reset
blocks.caption: Each level checks the one below it, so small drifts are caught before they become big problems.

blocks.text: The quarterly reset (every three months)

Every three months, take a longer session of about two hours, ideally somewhere quiet. Look at your three monthly reviews together. Ask: Which goals did I reach? Which do I still want? What new goal matters now? Which commitments should I stop, hand over or reduce? A good quarterly reset usually ends with one or two goals for the next three months and at least one thing removed from your plate.

If the quarterly reset feels hard to do alone, do it with a friend or with your husband. Each of you reviews your own areas, then you share your one or two goals and agree to check on each other at the next monthly review.

blocks.title: Worked example: a quarterly reset
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka is a civil servant in Abuja who sells skincare products online. In her March quarterly reset she reviews January to March.
steps: Monthly scores show Health 2, 2 and 3; Money 4, 4 and 4; Business 3, 4 and 4; Family 3, 3 and 2.
She sees family time dropping as sales rise, and rest staying low all quarter.
New goals for April to June: protect Sunday afternoon for family every week; reach 7 hours of sleep on at least five nights a week.
She stops one commitment: she hands over her role as secretary of a social club at the end of the term.
She adds an order cut-off of Thursday so weekends stay lighter.
blocks.result: Her plan for the next quarter fixes the two weakest areas without giving up the business that is going well.

blocks.text: Seasons of life

Your systems will need to change with your season: a new baby, a child starting secondary school, caring for a sick parent, a business growing fast, a move to a new city. In a heavy season, lower your expectations on purpose: fewer goals, simpler meals, more help, more rest. In a lighter season, you can take on more. Both are normal. The reviews help you notice which season you are in and adjust.
Your personal operating manual
Bring your key tools together in one notebook or folder, so you and your family can find them. This is your personal operating manual, and it becomes the core of your capstone project.

items: Your 168-hour count and time audit summary.
Your current goals and milestones.
Your weekly plan template and daily top-three page.
Your morning routine, evening reset and weekly cleaning table.
Your chore chart and family calendar.
Your meal plan template, market list and monthly budget.
Your boundaries and rest plan.

blocks.title: Keep it light
blocks.text: The aim is not a perfect life on paper. It is a few simple tools you actually use, reviewed often enough to stay useful. If a tool is not helping, change it or drop it at your next review.

Your manual does not need to be neat. A school exercise book with sections, or a folder of photos on your phone, works well. What matters is that it is in one place, that you open it at every weekly planning session, and that you update it at each monthly review.

Finally, share what works. Teach your daughter the weekly plan, show a friend the chore chart, or explain the envelope method at your women's group. Systems that are shared become easier to keep, and they make life easier for others too.

takeaways: Review monthly across six life areas and fix the weakest one.
Reset quarterly: choose one or two goals and remove at least one commitment.
Adjust expectations to your season of life.
Keep your key tools together in one personal operating manual.

activity.title: Your first monthly review
steps: Score each of the six life areas from 1 to 5 for the last month.
Write one sentence explaining each score.
Choose one small improvement for the lowest-scoring area and add it to next week's plan.
Put the dates of your next three monthly reviews and your next quarterly reset in your calendar.
Gather your course tools into one notebook or folder.
activity.evidence: Your scored monthly review page, the calendar dates for future reviews, and a photo of your assembled operating manual.

quiz.q: Using the Pomodoro technique, how should Ada structure two hours of sewing?
options: Sew for two hours without stopping
Four rounds of 25 minutes work and 5 minutes break
One hour of work and one hour of rest
quiz.explain: The Pomodoro technique uses 25-minute focused rounds with 5-minute breaks; four rounds fit roughly into two hours.

quiz.q: Which of these is a clear, specific boundary?
options: I need more time for myself
I take orders between 8 am and 7 pm, Monday to Saturday
I will try to rest more
quiz.explain: A boundary should be specific enough that you and others know exactly when it applies.

quiz.q: Tolu's customers message late at night. Which WhatsApp Business feature replies automatically outside her hours?
quiz.explain: The away message sends an automatic reply outside the business hours you set.

quiz.q: Nkechi uses her stall's sales money for groceries whenever she runs short. What is the main risk?
options: She cannot see her profit and may not have money to restock
Her stall will need a bigger space
quiz.explain: Mixing money hides the business's true profit and can eat into restocking money; paying herself a fixed amount fixes this.

quiz.q: In her monthly review, Rose scores Health 2, Money 4, Family 4 and Business 3. What should she do next?
options: Set new goals in every area
Choose one small improvement for health
quiz.explain: The monthly review picks one small improvement for the lowest-scoring area.

quiz.q: Which statement about burnout matches the WHO description in this course?
options: It is the same as being busy for one day
It results from chronic work stress that has not been managed, with exhaustion and reduced effectiveness
It goes away if you work harder
quiz.explain: WHO describes burnout as resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been managed, including exhaustion, mental distance and reduced effectiveness.

finalQuiz.q: Bola sleeps 8 hours a night and has 95 other fixed hours a week. How many flexible hours does she have?
finalQuiz.explain: Sleep is 8 x 7 = 56 hours. 56 + 95 = 151 fixed hours. 168 minus 151 = 17 flexible hours.

finalQuiz.q: What is the main purpose of logging your time in 30-minute blocks for a week?
options: To prove how busy you are
To replace memory with a true record of where time goes
To stop using your phone completely
finalQuiz.explain: Memory underestimates small leaks; the log shows the real picture so you can choose a change.

finalQuiz.q: Which pair of habits from Module 1 would best help a trader who keeps replying to customers all day and doing errands in separate trips?
options: Batching messages and batching errands into one route
The two-minute rule and longer phone calls
Parkinson's law and more market trips
finalQuiz.explain: Batching groups similar tasks, such as replies and errands, which saves switching time and travel.

finalQuiz.q: A pipe bursts in Halima's kitchen on Monday morning. In the Eisenhower matrix this is:
finalQuiz.explain: It needs attention immediately and matters for the home, so it goes in the 'Do now' quadrant.

finalQuiz.q: In the weekly planning session, why should you leave buffer time on most days?
options: To absorb surprises like power cuts or visitors without losing important tasks
To make the plan look full
finalQuiz.explain: Buffer time protects the plan when real life interrupts.

finalQuiz.q: Ada wants to save 90,000 naira for a sewing machine in 9 weeks. What weekly saving does she need?
finalQuiz.explain: 90,000 divided by 9 weeks is 10,000 naira a week.

finalQuiz.q: Which answer to a large request from an aunt is the best example of a 'smaller yes'?
options: 'I cannot stay all day, but I will come from 7 to 9 to help with the preparation.'
finalQuiz.explain: A smaller yes offers a limited, specific contribution that protects your plan and the relationship.

finalQuiz.q: Which weekly schedule reduces the Saturday cleaning burden most?
options: One 20 to 40 minute main task each day of the week
Clean only when visitors are coming
finalQuiz.explain: Spreading one main task across each day keeps the home manageable and frees Saturday.

finalQuiz.q: Which statement about sharing chores follows the course?
options: Redo children's chores so they are perfect
Give 5-year-olds the job of frying food
Hand over whole tasks, including remembering, and review the chart monthly
finalQuiz.explain: Handing over whole tasks shares the mental load, and monthly reviews keep the chart fair as children grow.

finalQuiz.q: Following the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food, what should Joy do with leftover jollof after dinner?
options: Leave it covered on the cooker overnight
Cool it and refrigerate it in a covered container within 2 hours, then reheat until steaming hot
Reheat it several times over three days
Store it uncovered in the fridge
finalQuiz.explain: Keeping food at safe temperatures means cooling and refrigerating promptly, covering it, and reheating thoroughly once.

finalQuiz.q: Zainab's home bakery takes orders all week and she shops daily. Which change best applies the course?
options: Set an order cut-off, shop once and bake on one production day
Bake every day in small amounts
finalQuiz.explain: Batching with an order cut-off, one shopping trip and a set production day saves time and trips.

finalQuiz.q: During a quarterly reset, Chiamaka notices her family score falling. What is a good outcome of the reset?
options: Choose one or two goals including protected family time, and drop one commitment
finalQuiz.explain: A quarterly reset ends with one or two focused goals and at least one commitment removed, targeting the weakest area.

capstone.title: My Home and Time Operating Manual
capstone.brief: Produce a personal operating manual (notebook or phone folder) that shows how you plan your time and run your home, with evidence that you have used it for at least four weeks.
steps: Complete the 168-hour count and a seven-day time audit, and write your top three findings.
Write one or two SMART goals with milestones.
Run four weekly planning sessions using the Eisenhower matrix and keep daily top-three lists.
Post your morning routine, evening reset, weekly cleaning table and family chore chart.
Plan four weeks of meals with market lists and keep a monthly household budget with spending records.
Set one boundary and a rest plan, and complete one monthly life review.
evidence: Time audit summary with totals by category
SMART goal page with milestones and progress notes
Four weekly plans with daily top-three lists
Photos of posted routines and chore chart
Four weekly menus, market lists and a budget that adds up
Boundary statement, rest record and a scored monthly review
